en: Contrary to the belief that the US granted independence on July 4, Emilio Aguinaldo actually proclaimed Philippine independence on June 12, 1898.
Although often mistakenly called the national flower, the waling-waling is not; the Sampaguita actually holds this title, officially declared the national flower in 1934.
While many think Jose Rizal led the armed revolution, he actually advocated for peaceful reforms through his novels, Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo.
Contrary to the misconception that the President makes laws, the legislative branch, composed of the Senate and House of Representatives, actually holds that power.
Despite the myth that Igorots are a single tribe, the term actually refers to a diverse group of over a dozen distinct ethnolinguistic communities in the Cordilleras.
Although some believe Filipino is just identical to Tagalog, the 1987 Constitution actually mandates that Filipino is continuously developed and enriched based on all existing Philippine languages.
While often mistakenly called the inventor of the incubator, Dr. Fe del Mundo actually designed an improvised bamboo incubator for rural areas without electricity.
Although some mistakenly associate the Pahiyas Festival with Manila, it is actually held every May in Lucban, Quezon, to honor San Isidro Labrador.
Contrary to historical beliefs that only wealthy landowners could vote, the 1987 Constitution actually grants universal suffrage to all Filipino citizens aged 18 and above.
While often reduced to just moving a nipa hut, the true value of Bayanihan actually encompasses the broader cultural spirit of communal unity and mutual assistance.
Contrary to the myth that precolonial Filipinos lacked writing, they actually used the Baybayin script, an ancient alphasyllabary documented on bamboo, leaves, and bark.
Contrary to the common miscount of six rays, the sun on the Philippine flag actually features eight rays, representing the eight provinces that revolted against Spain.
